plan.contextChunk: This figure comprises four reaction energy diagrams arranged in a two-by-two grid and labeled (a), (b), (c) and (d) at their upper left corners. Each panel carries a tall vertical arrow at its left shaded from cream to orange and labeled Energy, a pale blue plotting field, and beneath it a horizontal axis labeled Reaction progress ending in a magenta arrow pointing right; no numbers appear on either axis. Within every field a smooth magenta curve runs from a flat reactant level, over a single rounded maximum, and down to a flat product level. Horizontal dashed lines extend from the reactant level, the top of the maximum, and the product level, and double-headed vertical arrows between those dashed lines are labeled delta G with a double dagger for the barrier height and delta G degree for the overall change. Panel (a) pairs a low barrier with a product level well below the reactants. Panel (b) shows a tall barrier above the same downhill step, its drop to product smaller. Panel (c) has only a shallow hump and ends barely above the reactant level. Panel (d) combines a very tall barrier with a product level clearly above the reactants. Because axes and curve shape stay fixed across the grid, the panels isolate two independently varying quantities: barrier height, and whether products sit above or below reactants. The set establishes that every reaction has its own energy profile.

interactions.label: Reaction profile
interactions.teaches: Each profile combines two independent properties: a low or high activation barrier for speed, and a negative or positive ΔG° for thermodynamic direction

interactions.label: Activation barrier ΔG‡
interactions.teaches: Raising ΔG‡ makes the reaction slower without necessarily changing whether products are lower or higher in energy than reactants

demo_steps.title: Fast and exergonic
demo_steps.narration: The curve has a small hump and ends below the reactants. The low ΔG‡ indicates a fast reaction, while the negative ΔG° indicates products are thermodynamically favored.

demo_steps.title: Same downhill direction, slower reaction
demo_steps.narration: Increasing only the activation barrier makes the reaction slower, even though the product level remains below the reactants. Rate and favorability are not the same quantity.

demo_steps.title: Fast but endergonic
demo_steps.narration: A shallow barrier can still lead to products that sit above the reactants. This reaction may proceed quickly once started, but its positive ΔG° means products are not thermodynamically favored.

demo_steps.title: Slow and endergonic
demo_steps.narration: Here both quantities are unfavorable: the barrier is high and the products are higher in energy than the reactants. The profile combines a slow rate with positive ΔG°.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: ΔG‡ predicts how fast a reaction can occur, while ΔG° predicts whether products or reactants are lower in energy; the two can vary independently.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as four pale-blue reaction coordinate panels in a 2x2 grid, with orange vertical Energy arrows on the left and magenta Reaction progress arrows along the bottom. Keep axes unnumbered. Use one smooth magenta curve per panel: (a) low peak and product far below reactant, (b) high peak and product below reactant, (c) low peak and product slightly above reactant, and (d) high peak and product well above reactant. Dashed horizontal reference lines should align with reactant, peak, and product levels, with ΔG‡ shown from reactant to peak and ΔG° shown from reactant to product. The selected profile should be emphasized by an outline in the grid and duplicated or enlarged nearby, where the two energy arrows are highlighted in contrasting colors.

authoredContext:
Not all energy diagrams are like that shown for the reaction of ethylene and HBr. Each reaction has its own energy profile. Some reactions are fast (small ΔG‡) and some are slow (large ΔG‡); some have a negative ΔG°, and some have a positive ΔG°. The figure illustrates some different possibilities.

Some hypothetical energy diagrams: (a) a fast exergonic reaction (low ΔG‡, negative ΔG°); (b) a slow exergonic reaction (high ΔG‡, negative ΔG°); (c) a fast endergonic reaction (small ΔG‡, small positive ΔG°); (d) a slow endergonic reaction (high ΔG‡, positive ΔG°).

Four energy diagrams for different reactions with different values of delta G naught show different magnitudes of activation barrier.
